notes: Hook overclaim fixed: cutting one wire stops the engine only where the trip is de-energise-to-trip; research [61], [62], [69] say trips are typically built that way, but [68] records a normally de-energised shutdown that is not fail safe. Now "In many designs, cut one wire to a diesel generator's oil pressure trip and the engine stops...". The question it poses is unchanged and is answered by i8.
oneBreath narrowed: "most often a current sent round a two-wire loop" is a claim of prevalence no source makes; research [27]-[34] support the two-wire 4-20 mA loop only, so now "often".

oneBreath overclaim fixed: "every instrument is checked against a standard and set again"; a calibration may find an instrument within tolerance, and some instruments cannot be adjusted at all (lesson i1: a bad tape is replaced). Now "instruments are checked against a standard and, where needed, set again" (research [3], [8]).

oneBreath narrowed: "wired so that most faults in their own wiring fail safe" went beyond the research, which says a blown fuse or open circuit trips a de-energise-to-trip system [62], that alarms should fail to safety as far as practicable [63], and that some shutdown systems are not fail safe [68]. Now "usually wired so that a broken wire or a lost supply fails safe".

Rest checked: measure, compare, act matches i5 [35]-[40]; temperature, pressure, level and flow sensing matches i2 and i3 [12]-[26]; thermostat, PID and PLC logic match i5 to i7 [36]-[58]; agrees with lesson i1.
